item.title: Bay du Nord oil project clears final regulatory hurdle, awaits Equinor's next move
item.description: Equinor’s proposed Bay du Nord offshore oil project has cleared its final regulatory hurdle in Newfoundland and Labrador.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: ST. JOHN’S — Equinor’s proposed Bay du Nord offshore oil project has cleared its final regulatory hurdle in Newfoundland and Labrador. Officials with the federal and provincial governments announced today they had accepted the development’s approval by the Canada-Newfoundland and Labrador Offshore Energy Regulator. Premier Tony Wakeham says the approval was an important milestone ahead of Equinor’s final decision next year on whether it will proceed with the project. He said his government is still considering whether to buy a 10 per cent stake in the $14-billion development. Bay du Nord would be the first deepwater oil development in Canada, and farther from shore than any other oil project on Earth. Norway-based Equinor would drill wells more than a kilometre below the surface of the ocean, in waters about 500 kilometres northeast of St. John’s, N.L. The company expects to extract more than 400 million barrels of oil, with first oil expected in 2031. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

item.title: Global shares drop on AI worries, echoing Wall Street's decline despite the strong Anthropic debut
item.description: Global shares dropped in Friday trading as a wide selloff hits issues related to artificial intelligence and computer chips.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7 per cent, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year. The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a “correction,” having fallen more than 10 per cent from its Oct. 6 all-time high. The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration’s trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3 per cent, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9 per cent. Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1 per cent. The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell more than 5 per cent overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well. AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market. The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks’ big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data centre construction winning at both the federal and state level. “The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that’s what’s being priced right now,” said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. “But I don’t think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over.” Much of the AI rout was centreed among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centres. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3 per cent, Micron Technology slid 13.9 per cent and Broadcom fell 12.1 per cent. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7 per cent. Corning slid 10.9 per cent and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3 per cent. Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8 per cent lower. The chip company’s stock was caught up in the market’s anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25 per cent. The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.1 per cent to US$88.30, but remains above its IPO price of US$83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing US$2 trillion in value. Anthropic’s share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23 per cent decline from its brief peak of US$115.10 a share set the day prior. That’s an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO. Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50 per cent in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later. Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7 per cent and homebuilder Lennar gained 1 per cent. All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73. While the stock market’s mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year. The University of Michigan’s latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists’ expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran. Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93 per cent from 5.04 per cent late Thursday. Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6 per cent to settle at US$92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil. ___ Damian J. Troise and Alex Veiga, The Associated Press AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

item.title: There is no going back 'to the way it was before' the Iran war's energy shock, IEA says
item.description: The world’s largest energy shock in history and growing climate change concerns this year are reshaping the future of how people will power homes, drive cars and fuel industries, according to an ...
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: The world’s largest energy shock in history and growing climate change concerns this year are reshaping the future of how people will power homes, drive cars and fuel industries, according to an International Energy Agency report released Thursday. The energy crisis, triggered by the Iran war, will “leave lasting marks” on the world’s energy sector, according to the Paris-based IEA, founded after the 1973-74 energy crisis. Energy-hungry nations will prioritize the security and affordability of their electricity, the report said. This is a boon for renewable technologies, like solar, and alternative technologies, like nuclear. But it is also reinforcing the case to keep coal as a backup in times of crisis. This is especially true in coal-rich Asia, which went into energy triage when the Iran war cut off the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow passageway where around a fifth of the world’s traded oil typically flows. The report looks “past the current turmoil to explore the range of energy futures that could emerge from today’s upheaval,” said IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol. He said the Iran war “delivered a huge shock to the system” and warned “the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be.” “I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” he said. Annual United Nations climate talks, known as COP31 and hosted in Turkiye this year, are in their second and final week. Before these negotiations, the UN announced the world is dangerously close to missing its goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures. Electrification — the process of powering homes, cars and industries with electricity — and moving away from planet-warming fossil fuels are the two big ticket issues at this year’s climate talks. “The future of the energy system and our climate are inextricably intertwined,” said Rachel Cleetus, climate program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists, who is at COP31. Flagship report forecasts energy future The IEA, the world’s leading intergovernmental energy organization with more than 30 member countries, publishes World Energy Outlooks annually. This year’s 560-page plus report analyzes government and private data to project various future scenarios based on whether countries will continue with current policies or drastically change policies in the face of ongoing crises. The world’s energy sector will clearly have a before and after the Iran war, experts said. In March, the IEA coordinated the emergency release of 400 million barrels of crude oil stocks to stabilize global markets. “This crisis has exposed the price of fossil fuel dependence,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa. “It’s crazy that a conflict thousands of miles away can send energy bills soaring at home.” Conflicts, trade tensions, climate risks and cyberattacks are increasing the number of possible energy futures. The IEA said the “drive to diversify” fuel supplies will reshape the energy trade. The Middle East will still be the world’s largest oil exporter, but nations will likely reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz. The IEA forecasts the amount of oil transiting the strait could go from 20 million barrels per day before the Iran war, to 8.5 million barrels in 2030, and even under 2 million barrels by 2035. While fossil fuels still dominate national energy mixes, the IEA said renewables — led by solar — and nuclear power are the “biggest beneficiaries” of governments trying to grow domestic energy sources. But energy security concerns may lead coal-rich nations to rely on the fossil fuel as a fallback option during times of crisis. “When we look at how energy crises change the world over the long term, governments are only just beginning to get their head around just how much things will change,” said Dave Jones, co-founder of the think tank Ember. Climate talks eye electrification The ongoing talks in Turkiye follow a year rattled by the Iran war’s energy shock, as well as several climate-induced disasters. Global warming adds pressure to rising electricity demand. In what the IEA called a “striking milestone,” energy demand for cooling is overtaking energy demand for heating for the first time. India, the world’s most populous nation, will account for more energy demand growth over the next decade than any other country or region. China, already one of the world’s most electrified economies, may see its electrification grow from 32 per cent last year to 43 per cent by 2035 — the highest among any major economy. At COP31, Turkiye is pushing for the world to increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21 per cent today to 35 per cent by 2035. While the preference would be for this to come from renewable energy, UN documents on the negotiating table don’t spell this out. That means coal and other fossil fuels could be used, at least initially. “The IEA’s latest report makes clear that the fossil energy crisis unleashed by the U.S.-Israel war on Iran has irrevocably changed the global energy system, adding to the many reasons why countries would benefit from a rapid transition to clean energy and electrification,” said Cleetus, with the Union of Concerned Scientists. ___ The Associated Press’ climate and environmental coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. The AP is solely responsible for all content. Find AP’s standards for working with philanthropies, a list of supporters and funded coverage areas at AP.org. Anton L. Delgado and Sibi Arasu, The Associated Press Delgado reported from Bangkok and Arasu from Bengaluru, India.
